title: Knit through the back loop (k tbl)
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 351. Public domain. Method also described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright in UK/EU.

glossaryTerms.definition: Abbreviation for 'knit through the back loop'. The needle enters the back leg of the stitch, twisting it as it is worked.
A deliberate wrap of the yarn over the needle between stitches, creating a new loop and, in lace, an intentional hole.
An increase worked by lifting the horizontal bar between two stitches onto the left needle and knitting into it, usually through the back loop to avoid a hole.
The number of stitches and rows per 10 cm in a given yarn on a given needle size. Called 'gauge' in US knitting.

content.text: The secret of knit through the back loop (abbreviated
k tbl

) is that entering the stitch from the back rotates the stitch so the legs cross. This makes a tighter, more upright column than a plain knit. The twist happens because the needle enters at a different angle. It is not a fluke.
You need yarn and needles. Cast on a small swatch of 10 to 15 stitches in any weight. The contrast between a plain knit column and a k tbl column is clearest in a smooth, plied yarn.

content.text: Step by step
Bring the right needle to the back of the work and insert it into the stitch from right to left through the back leg of the loop (the leg sitting behind the left needle).
The right needle tip will point away from you and slightly to the left. The entry feels more restricted than a standard knit stitch; that is correct.
Wrap the yarn around the right needle in the usual direction (anticlockwise from above).
Draw the new loop through the back of the stitch and slide the old stitch off the left needle.
The completed stitch sits twisted on the needle with its legs crossed. In the finished fabric this reads as a denser, more defined stitch than the one beside it.
Where you'll see it

k tbl appears in twisted rib, where knit stitches on right-side rows are worked k tbl to keep the columns crisp. Some Eastern European and Middle Eastern traditions work all knit stitches through the back loop. It is also used as a single-stitch fix after a
yarn over
that would otherwise leave a hole. It also shows up in some
make-one increase
instructions where the lifted bar is worked through the back loop to close the increase neatly.
Common faults

Working the front leg instead of the back leg. If the stitch on the needle looks the same as a plain knit stitch in the finished fabric, check your entry point. The needle should enter at the back of the needle, not the front.
Dropped stitch when drawing the loop through. The restricted angle makes the draw-through slightly harder. Keep the stitch close to the tip of the left needle so there is less distance to travel.
Tighter overall fabric. k tbl consistently tightens
tension
by roughly half a stitch per 10 cm compared with plain knit. If a pattern calls for a full section of twisted stitches, re-swatch with a larger needle size.
What to try next: pair k tbl with
purl through the back loop
to work a full twisted rib.
